messages.subject: DTF/DIF in quasi-experimental design: What to do with items with DIF?
messages.subject_clean: DTF/DIF in quasi-experimental design: What to do with items with DIF?
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I’m writing here because I’ve been struggling to find good literature on DIF/DTF analysis in controlled experiments, and I’m hoping you can help.

For my PhD, I’m using a quasi-experimental design with two intervention groups and one control group. I’m measuring (mathematical) abilities at three points: Pre, Post, and Follow-Up, using the same 11-item test for all groups and time points, analyzed with a unidimensional graded response model (GRM).

To make sure I can confidently use the scale across groups and time points (and later run regression analyses), I decided to check for measurement invariance. The way I see it, I only need to compare two groups:
1. Students with no instruction in the subject (all groups at Pretest and the control group at all time points).
2. Students who’ve received instruction (Post and Follow-Up for the intervention groups).

I ran DIF and DTF (DRF) analyses for these two groups (all in all N=710) and found three items with DIF, as well as significant unsigned DRF (but not significant signed DRF). Results are included below.

Now, I’m unsure about two things:
1. Does my approach to grouping and running the analyses make sense?
2. What should I do with the items showing DIF?

I’m not keen on dropping them. Should I try a model with group-specific GRM parameters (as suggested by Liu & Rogers, 2022, DOI: 10.1177/00131644211012050)? Or would it be okay to assume the DTF reflects something inherent to students who have or haven’t had instruction and thus just ignore it?

I’d really appreciate your thoughts and advice!

Thanks a lot

Martin

messages.subject: Re: simdata() results in different population H coefficients
messages.subject_clean: simdata() results in different population H coefficients
messages.body_plain:
It looks like you're using the classical IRT parameterization (a-b) rather than the slope intercept version (a-d). If you transform the parameters first for simdata() that should work.

Phil

On Wed, Oct 9, 2024 at 4:58 PM Sebastian Lortz <s.a.j...@student.rug.nl> wrote:

> Dear Phil and everybody in this group,
>
> Thanks for accepting my joining request.
> I have outcomes of the simdata() function I cannot explain despite studying the references for the  mirt package. I would be very thankful for your help.
> I am conducting a simulation study on H coefficients and use mirt for simulating the data sets. I noted that the exact population H coefficients I calculate (via integration) based on a and b parameters are constantly different (+.03-.05) from the estimated H coefficients (mokken::coefH()) based on data from mirt::simdata(a = rep(1.5,5), d = seq(-1,1, length.out = 5), N = 1000000, itemtype = "2PL").
>
> I tried to understand how simdata() works and used base R for simulating:
> # set parameters
>
> a = rep(1.5,5)
>
> b = seq(-1, 1, length.out = 5)
>
> n = 1000000
>
> ni = length(a)
>
> # simulating population with base R
>
> pl2 <- function (theta, a, b) {
>
>   p <- exp(1.0*a*(theta-b)) / (1+exp(1.0*a*(theta-b)))
>
>   return(
>
>     p
>
>   )}
>
> # take a random sample of size n, create data frame
>
> theta <- rnorm(n)
>
> data <- data.frame(theta)
>
> # calculate probabilities based on theta, a, b.
>
> for (i2 in 1:ni) {
>
>   # define item difficulty and open item vector
>
>   bi = b[i2]
>
>   ai = a[i2]
>
>   item = c()
>
>   # apply pl2 function over every theta
>
>   for (i in 1:n) {
>
>     p <- pl2(theta = theta[i],a = ai, b = bi)
>
>       item[i] <- rbinom(1,1,p)
>
>     }
>
>   # attach item to data
>
>   data <- cbind(data,item)
>
> }
>
>
> The H coefficients I estimate from my base R simulation match the exact population H I calculated. So my questions is, how is that possible and where exactly does the simdata() function different steps than I do using base R.
>
>
> Thanks in advance!
>
> I attach an example script if necessary.
>
>
> All the best
>
> Sebastian

messages.subject: Re: mirt vs. lavaan
messages.body_plain:
This is largely for numerical integration reasons as 0-1 scaling is easier to set up a grid for. If you want  the parameters to be more comparable, set the variance of the latent traits in lavaan to 1 and estimate the first slope. I hosted a simulation comparing the two packages, which you may find helpful: http://philchalmers.github.io/SimDesign/html/03-Parameter_recovery_simulation.html

Phil

messages.subject: Re: Error generating empirical plot in vertical scaling (subscript out of bounds)
messages.subject_clean: Error generating empirical plot in vertical scaling (subscript out of bounds)
messages.body_plain:
This looks to be a bug, but a predictable one. You really can't build an empirical plot for a given item when all the responses within a group are NAs. It should however be possible to take a group subset via extract.group() and plot the items that way....

Phil

messages.subject: Re: DIF with drop_sequential scheme
messages.body_plain:
It's important with the drop schemes to leave at least one item as an anchor throughout, otherwise the model will lose its scaling identification. Use the items2test input and leave out one item you're fairly certain is invariance across groups and go from there, or stick with the 'drop' scheme and perform the wave searches manually. HTH.

Phil

messages.subject: Re: Nominal model and parameter constrains
messages.body_plain:
Hi Regina,

I think setting up the first 1-4 categories with scoring coefficients that mimic the GPCM would make sense (0, 1,2,3, respectively), while leaving the last category as something that is estimable would be the most reasonable. Something like this:

################
> library(mirt)
>
> head(Science)
  Comfort Work Future Benefit
1       4    4      3       2
2       3    3      3       3
3       3    2      2       3
4       3    2      2       3
5       3    4      4       1
6       4    4      3       3
>
> # Item 1 is structured item in question
> baseline_mod <- mirt(Science, itemtype = c('nominal', rep('graded', 3)))
Iteration: 59, Log-Lik: -1607.205, Max-Change: 0.00009
> coef(baseline_mod)[[1]]
          a1 ak0     ak1    ak2 ak3 d0       d1       d2       d3
par 1.071035   0 1.60566 2.0477   3  0 3.912586 6.183833 4.806511
>
> # assume category 1-3 in item 1 are ordered, while the last could be unordered
> mod <- mirt(Science, itemtype = c('nominal', rep('graded', 3)),
+             model = "Theta = 1-4
+             FIXED = (1, ak0), (1, ak1), (1, ak2),
+             START = (1, ak0, 0), (1, ak1, 1), (1, ak2, 2)
+             FREE = (1,ak3)")
Iteration: 58, Log-Lik: -1608.227, Max-Change: 0.00010
> coef(mod)[[1]]
           a1 ak0 ak1 ak2      ak3 d0       d1      d2       d3
par 0.7146897   0   1   2 3.422804  0 2.583246 4.99544 3.610593
>
> # models effectively the same (more constrained preferred)
> anova(mod, baseline_mod)
                  AIC    SABIC       HQ      BIC    logLik    X2 df     p
mod          3250.453 3264.024 3277.210 3317.965 -1608.227
baseline_mod 3250.411 3264.780 3278.741 3321.894 -1607.205 2.042  1 0.153

############

Regarding the fit statistics, the df have more to do with the number of items and parameters, where too few items can cause problems as the number of moments is too low. Also note that the na.rm argument is no longer required as the fit statistics now use MAR assumptions (and therefore no row-wise deletion is required). HTH.

Phil
